carePlan.urgentPriorityText: Your latest result includes an urgent flag. Follow the recommendation promptly and contact a clinician if symptoms are getting worse.
carePlan.routinePriorityText: Your latest result does not show an urgent flag. Continue with the recommended follow-up and monitor any symptom changes.
carePlan.noSymptoms: No symptoms reported in your latest assessment.
carePlan.numbersNoLabs: No lab values yet — a fasting glucose and HbA1c test will make your reports far more accurate.
carePlan.understandingConfirmed: Your results meet the criteria for diabetes. This is not an emergency — it means your blood sugar has been consistently above the normal range. The next step is a care plan: meet your clinician, set sugar targets, and start treatment, plus regular eye and foot checks.
carePlan.understandingPossible: Your answers match common signs of diabetes, but a blood test is still needed to confirm. Book a fasting glucose or HbA1c test — it takes minutes and any lab can do it.
carePlan.understandingPrediabetes: Your numbers sit in the borderline range between normal and diabetes. This stage can often be reversed: about 7% weight loss, 150 minutes of activity a week, and fewer sugary drinks sharply lower the risk.
carePlan.understandingGestational: Your results relate to diabetes in pregnancy. Pregnancy changes how the body handles sugar. Your obstetric team will plan glucose monitoring and diet first — with good control, most pregnancies go well.
carePlan.understandingLowRisk: No strong diabetes signs were found in your latest assessment. Keep your healthy routines, re-check routinely every 1–3 years, and come back sooner if new symptoms appear.
carePlan.understandingType1: Your pattern (rapid onset with weight loss) fits type 1 diabetes, where the body stops making insulin. This needs specialist care quickly — insulin treatment cannot wait for a routine appointment.
carePlan.understandingMixed: Your results show features of more than one diabetes type. A clinician may order extra antibody tests to pick the right treatment.
carePlan.understandingFallback: This report compares your answers against medical rules for diabetes. Open the full report to see the evidence behind it and the recommended next steps.
carePlan.warningBody: Go to emergency care for fruity-smelling breath, deep or fast breathing, vomiting with no fluids kept down, confusion or extreme drowsiness. For shakiness, sweating or dizziness, take fast sugar (juice or glucose tablets) and recheck after 15 minutes.

recommendations.hypoSignsTitle: Know how to treat low blood sugar
recommendations.hypoSignsText: Shakiness, sweating or dizziness can mean low blood sugar. If it happens, take fast-acting sugar (juice, glucose tablets) and tell your clinician.
recommendations.veryHighGlucoseText: A reading of {{value}} mg/dL needs medical attention soon. Contact your clinician, drink water, and avoid sugary drinks for now.
recommendations.missingLabsTitle: Add lab tests to unlock better insight
recommendations.missingLabsText: Your assessments have no lab values yet. A fasting glucose and HbA1c test would make your reports and these recommendations far more accurate.
recommendations.diabetesRangeGlucoseTitle: Discuss your glucose with a clinician
recommendations.diabetesRangeGlucoseText: Your fasting glucose of {{value}} mg/dL is in the diabetes range. Book an appointment to confirm the result and plan next steps.
recommendations.prediabetesGlucoseText: Your glucose of {{value}} mg/dL is in the warning range. Diet changes and regular movement now can bring it back to normal.
recommendations.a1cElevatedText: Your HbA1c of {{value}}% is above target. A check every 3 months shows whether your plan is actually working.
recommendations.weightManagementText: A BMI of {{value}} responds well to small changes: balanced portions and a daily walk. Even a 5% weight loss measurably improves glucose.
recommendations.underweightText: A BMI of {{value}} is below the healthy range. Focus on nutrient-rich meals and ask a professional about a safe plan to gain weight.
recommendations.symptomDiaryText: You reported {{count}} symptoms ({{symptoms}}). Note when they appear and how strong they feel — it helps your clinician spot patterns.
recommendations.quitSmokingTitle: Quit smoking to protect your vessels
recommendations.quitSmokingText: Smoking sharply raises the risk of diabetes complications. Ask your clinician about cessation support — it's one of the highest-impact changes you can make.
recommendations.reassessSoonText: Your last check was {{days}} days ago. Re-run the assessment to keep your report and trends up to date.
recommendations.bpMonitorTitle: Check your blood pressure at home
recommendations.bpMonitorText: You flagged hypertension. Measure twice a week at rest and bring the readings to your appointments.
recommendations.yearlyScreeningText: Your risk factors make yearly glucose checks important — even when you feel completely fine.
recommendations.buildHistoryText: You've completed {{count}} assessment(s). Repeating the assessment monthly reveals trends and makes every report smarter.
recommendations.stayActiveText: Brisk walking, cycling or swimming lowers glucose and improves insulin sensitivity. Start with 10-minute walks after meals.
recommendations.balancedDietText: Half vegetables, a quarter protein, a quarter whole grains — and water instead of sweet drinks. Simple habits, big effect on glucose.

prevention.sectionSubtitle: Evidence-based lifestyle interventions and clinical goals tailored to your result.

prediabetes.title: Prediabetes (Impaired Glucose Regulation)
prediabetes.tagline: Active Metabolic Reversal & Progression Prevention Strategy
prediabetes.goalBadge: Goal: Reverse HbA1c to < 5.7% & 5–7% Weight Loss
checklist: Schedule confirmatory Fasting Plasma Glucose and HbA1c laboratory testing within 30 days.
Adopt the Diabetes Prevention Plate Method (50% non-starchy vegetables, 25% lean protein, 25% whole grains).
Engage in at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic physical activity per week.
Target a 5% to 7% reduction in body weight if currently overweight or BMI > 25 kg/m².
Schedule a medical consultation with your doctor or dietitian to build a personalized prevention roadmap.

nutrition.title: Metabolic Plate & Carbohydrate Optimization
nutrition.focus: Low Glycemic Index, High Soluble Fiber & Zero Sugary Drinks
items: Fill half your plate with non-starchy greens (spinach, broccoli, cucumbers) to blunt glycemic spikes.
Completely substitute refined white sugars and sweetened beverages with water, unsweetened green tea, or sparkling water.
Pair all carbohydrates with protein or healthy fats (nuts, seeds, olive oil) to slow digestion and prevent surges.

activity.title: Cardio Resistance & Post-Meal Movement
items: Take a brisk 10–15 minute walk immediately after your largest meal to activate insulin-independent glucose clearance.
Accumulate 30 minutes of moderate cardio (brisk walking, cycling, swimming) at least 5 days every week.
Incorporate 2 days of bodyweight or resistance training weekly to build muscle glycogen storage capacity.

milestones.day30: Establish consistent daily dietary habits and log baseline fasting glucose readings.
milestones.day90: Repeat HbA1c laboratory screening; expect 0.2%–0.5% drop with sustained lifestyle intervention.
milestones.month6: Comprehensive physician review, lipid panel check, and reassessment of cardiovascular risk factors.
milestones.year1: Annual oral glucose tolerance or HbA1c test to certify sustained metabolic normalcy.

routine.morning: Check fasting glucose if advised, eat a protein and fiber-rich breakfast, and do a 10-minute stretch.
routine.afternoon: Enjoy a balanced fiber-dense lunch, followed by a 15-minute brisk walk to blunt post-meal spikes.
routine.evening: Nutrient-rich dinner with leafy greens and lean protein; eliminate late-night snacking.
routine.bedtime: Wind down with water or herbal tea, review daily activity goals, and aim for 7–8 hours of sound sleep.

prediabetes.insight: Clinical trials from the Diabetes Prevention Program (DPP) demonstrate that comprehensive lifestyle modification reduces the risk of progressing to Type 2 diabetes by 58% (and 71% in adults aged 60+).

type2.title: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
type2.tagline: Glycemic Control, Organ Protection & Complication Prevention
checklist: Schedule an appointment with your primary care clinician or endocrinologist to finalize your treatment plan.
Routinely monitor and record your fasting and 2-hour postprandial blood glucose as prescribed.
Adhere strictly to all prescribed antihyperglycemic medications (such as Metformin, SGLT2i, or GLP-1 RA).
Complete comprehensive baseline labs: HbA1c, lipid panel, kidney function (eGFR, uACR), and dilated eye exam.
Perform daily foot examinations for sores, blisters, or temperature changes, and protect feet with proper footwear.

nutrition.title: Carbohydrate Management & Vascular Health
nutrition.focus: Consistent Carb Distribution, Lean Proteins & Heart-Healthy Fats
items: Maintain consistent carbohydrate portions across meals to avoid wide swings in daytime blood glucose.
Emphasize whole foods: legumes, leafy vegetables, berries, and omega-3 fatty fish (salmon, sardines).
Limit dietary sodium to < 2,300 mg/day and minimize saturated fats to protect cardiovascular and renal health.

activity.title: Aerobic Conditioning & Muscle Glycogen Depletion
items: Perform at least 150 minutes weekly of moderate-to-vigorous aerobic exercise without going more than 2 consecutive days without activity.
Perform resistance training 2–3 times per week targeting all major muscle groups to boost insulin sensitivity.
Avoid prolonged sitting; break up sedentary periods every 30 minutes with 2–3 minutes of walking or standing.

milestones.day30: Review glucose log with your healthcare team and adjust medication dosages if targets are not met.
milestones.day90: Quarterly HbA1c check and assessment of glycemic variability and medication tolerance.
milestones.month6: Comprehensive metabolic review, blood pressure check, and lifestyle habit reinforcement.
milestones.year1: Annual dilated retinal eye exam, comprehensive podiatry exam, and microalbuminuria urine test.

routine.morning: Check fasting blood sugar, take morning diabetes medication as prescribed, and enjoy a low-GI breakfast.
routine.afternoon: Balanced lunch, take a 15–20 minute walk to manage postprandial glucose, and stay well hydrated.
routine.evening: Portion-controlled dinner with complex carbs, take evening medication, and log your post-meal reading.
routine.bedtime: Inspect both feet for cuts, redness, or blisters; prepare tomorrow's supplies; maintain restful sleep.

type2.insight: Maintaining HbA1c below 7.0% significantly reduces microvascular complications (retinopathy, neuropathy, nephropathy) by up to 40% and slows cardiovascular progression.

type1.title: Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus
type1.tagline: Precision Insulin Replacement & Acute Complication Defense
type1.goalBadge: Goal: Time in Range (TIR 70-180 mg/dL) > 70% & DKA Prevention
checklist: Consult urgently with an endocrinologist for comprehensive insulin regimen formulation and diabetes education.
Master basal-bolus insulin administration, timing, and individual carbohydrate-to-insulin (I:C) ratios.
Check blood glucose 4–10 times daily, or set up and calibrate a Continuous Glucose Monitor (CGM).
Keep fast-acting carbohydrates (15g glucose tablets, fruit juice) with you at all times for hypoglycemia treatment.
Obtain blood or urine ketone testing supplies and establish a clear sick-day management protocol to prevent DKA.

nutrition.title: Accurate Carbohydrate Counting & Bolus Matching
nutrition.focus: Carb-to-Insulin Matching, Glycemic Index Awareness & Hypo Readiness
items: Accurately calculate total grams of carbohydrates per meal to administer the correct pre-meal bolus dose.
Account for high-protein and high-fat meals which can cause delayed glucose rises 3–5 hours after eating.
Follow the Rule of 15 for hypoglycemia: consume 15g fast sugar, wait 15 minutes, recheck, and repeat if < 70 mg/dL.

activity.title: Safe Exercise & Glycemic Trend Management
activity.focus: Pre-Exercise Glucose Planning, CGM Alerts & Hypo Prevention
items: Check blood glucose or CGM arrows before starting exercise; consume 15–30g carbs if glucose is < 90–100 mg/dL.
Keep emergency fast-acting glucose, snacks, and a glucagon rescue kit accessible during all workouts.
Note that anaerobic/sprint exercise may temporarily spike glucose while prolonged cardio tends to lower it.

milestones.day30: Review CGM Ambulatory Glucose Profile (AGP) or glucose logs with diabetes educator to refine insulin sensitivity factors.
milestones.day90: Quarterly HbA1c test and CGM Time-in-Range (TIR) analysis; verify severe hypoglycemia frequency is < 1%.
milestones.month6: Endocrine specialist follow-up, injection site inspection (checking for lipohypertrophy), and thyroid function screening.
milestones.year1: Annual screening for celiac disease, thyroid antibodies, diabetic retinopathy, and urine microalbumin.

routine.morning: Check fasting glucose/CGM, calculate insulin bolus for breakfast carbs, administer dose 10–15 mins before eating.
routine.afternoon: Pre-lunch glucose check, calculate carb ratio for lunch, ensure hypo rescue supplies are in your bag.
routine.evening: Pre-dinner glucose test, administer mealtime insulin, verify bedtime basal dose timing.
routine.bedtime: Check glucose before sleep (target 100–140 mg/dL to prevent nighttime lows), keep juice/glucose tabs at bedside.

type1.insight: Utilizing Continuous Glucose Monitoring (CGM) combined with structured carbohydrate matching improves Time in Range (70-180 mg/dL) while minimizing both severe hypoglycemia and ketoacidosis.

gestational.title: Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM)
gestational.tagline: Maternal-Fetal Metabolic Health & Safe Pregnancy Protocol
checklist: Schedule an urgent visit with your obstetrician and a maternal-fetal diabetes educator.
Monitor and log blood glucose 4 times daily: fasting and 1 hour (or 2 hours) after each main meal.
Work with a prenatal registered dietitian to design an eating plan that supports healthy fetal growth.
Engage in safe, moderate physical activity (such as a 15-minute walk after meals) with obstetric clearance.
Schedule a repeat 75g Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT) at 4 to 12 weeks postpartum.

nutrition.title: Prenatal Glycemic Nutrition & Steady Energy
nutrition.focus: Complex Carbohydrates, Adequate Fetal Fuel & Protein Balance
items: Distribute carbohydrates evenly across 3 moderate meals and 2–3 small snacks to avoid high glucose spikes.
Prioritize whole grains, dairy, legumes, and lean poultry while avoiding concentrated fruit juices and syrups.
Include a bedtime snack with protein and complex carbs (e.g. Greek yogurt or peanut butter on whole wheat) to prevent morning ketones.

activity.title: Pregnancy-Safe Physical Movement
activity.focus: Low-Impact Cardio, Pelvic Health & Post-Meal Walks
items: Take a gentle 10–15 minute walk after breakfast, lunch, and dinner to stimulate muscle glucose uptake.
Engage in prenatal swimming, stationary cycling, or guided prenatal yoga 3–4 days per week.
Stay well-hydrated, avoid overheating, and stop immediately if experiencing dizziness, contractions, or shortness of breath.

milestones.day30: Evaluate maternal glucose logs with your obstetrician; determine if insulin or oral therapy is required.
milestones.day90: Monitor fetal growth ultrasounds for macrosomia and amniotic fluid levels; maintain strict glucose logs.
milestones.month6: Delivery planning with obstetric team; establish intrapartum blood glucose protocol.
milestones.year1: Postpartum 4–12 week 75g OGTT screening, followed by annual diabetes screening for maternal prevention.

routine.morning: Check fasting blood sugar upon waking, eat a balanced prenatal breakfast, and record reading in your log.
routine.afternoon: Check 1-hr post-lunch glucose, take a gentle 15-minute walk, and enjoy a healthy mid-afternoon snack.
routine.evening: Nutritious dinner with balanced carbs and protein, check 1-hr post-dinner glucose, and stay hydrated.
routine.bedtime: Eat a recommended bedtime snack (complex carb + protein) to maintain overnight glucose stability.

gestational.insight: Maintaining tight maternal glucose targets prevents macrosomia (large birth weight), neonatal hypoglycemia, and significantly lowers long-term metabolic risks for both child and mother.

no_strong_indication.title: Low Risk / No Strong Indication of Diabetes
no_strong_indication.tagline: Proactive Metabolic Wellness & Long-Term Prevention Protocol
no_strong_indication.goalBadge: Goal: Maintain Optimal Insulin Sensitivity & Vitality
checklist: Continue your healthy lifestyle habits with balanced, whole-food nutrition and daily movement.
Schedule routine annual preventative wellness check-ups and fasting metabolic screenings.
Stay aware of subtle warning signs such as excessive thirst, frequent nighttime urination, or unexplained fatigue.
Prioritize 7 to 8 hours of restorative sleep each night to maintain optimal cellular insulin sensitivity.
Retake this assessment whenever your health metrics, body weight, or symptom profile changes.

nutrition.title: Proactive Metabolic & Whole-Food Nutrition
nutrition.focus: Mediterranean Pattern, High Fiber & Minimally Processed Foods
items: Base your daily diet on whole, unprocessed foods: vegetables, fruits, legumes, whole grains, nuts, and extra virgin olive oil.
Avoid sugary beverages, energy drinks, and ultra-processed snacks to protect metabolic flexibility.
Stay well hydrated with 2 liters of water daily, supporting natural metabolic clearance and digestive health.

activity.title: Functional Fitness & Lifelong Movement
items: Aim for at least 150–300 minutes of moderate aerobic activity (e.g. brisk walking, jogging, cycling) each week.
Incorporate strength and resistance training 2–3 times weekly to maintain muscle mass and metabolic rate.
Practice daily active habits: take the stairs, walk during phone calls, and minimize continuous screen sitting.

milestones.day30: Review current diet and exercise habits to reinforce sustainable, enjoyable daily health routines.
milestones.day90: Check in on fitness benchmarks, energy levels, resting heart rate, and body composition.
milestones.month6: Mid-year wellness self-check: verify weight stability, blood pressure, and symptom-free vitality.
milestones.year1: Annual physical examination, comprehensive blood chemistry panel, and metabolic risk reassessment.

routine.morning: Hydrate with a tall glass of water, enjoy a balanced fiber-rich breakfast, and engage in morning movement.
routine.afternoon: Wholesome lunch with diverse vegetables and protein, take a 10-minute stretch or walk outside.
routine.evening: Light home-cooked dinner, unwind with relaxing activities or light physical recreation.
routine.bedtime: Limit screen exposure 30 minutes before sleep, relax in a cool room, and rest 7–8 hours.

no_strong_indication.insight: Maintaining normal metabolic markers through lifelong whole-food nutrition and consistent physical activity prevents over 90% of type 2 diabetes cases.

urgent.title: Urgent Clinical Attention Needed
urgent.tagline: Immediate Medical Assessment & Emergency Stabilisation Protocol
urgent.goalBadge: Goal: Urgent Clinical Triage & Immediate Medical Safety
checklist: Seek immediate medical evaluation or emergency care for acute symptoms or extreme glucose levels.
Do not drive yourself to the hospital if experiencing dizziness, confusion, weakness, or vision changes.
Bring all current medications, prior lab results, and symptom history to the emergency or urgent care clinic.
Maintain hydration with small sips of water unless vomiting or instructed otherwise by medical personnel.
Follow all physician triage instructions strictly and schedule immediate follow-up care.

nutrition.title: Emergency Stabilization Hydration
nutrition.focus: Medical Direction, Hydration Safety & Avoiding Extreme Sugars
items: Follow immediate instructions from medical personnel regarding food and fluid intake.
If experiencing hypoglycemia (shaking, sweating, confusion), consume 15g fast sugar immediately.
If blood sugar is severely elevated, drink plain water and avoid all juices, sodas, and heavy carbohydrates.

activity.title: Rest & Vital Sign Monitoring
activity.focus: Complete Rest, Avoid Exertion & Emergency Contact Access
items: Cease all strenuous exercise immediately; rest in a safe, seated or lying position.
Have a family member, friend, or coworker stay with you while arranging medical transportation.
Keep your emergency medical contacts and phone readily accessible at all times.

milestones.day30: Attend required post-emergency follow-up consultation and review adjusted medication regimen.
milestones.day90: Comprehensive secondary prevention review and stabilization assessment with specialist.
milestones.month6: Cardiometabolic status check and evaluation of ongoing safety protocols.
milestones.year1: Annual specialized clinical audit and preventive care maintenance.

routine.morning: Check symptoms and glucose immediately; adhere to urgent physician recommendations without delay.
routine.afternoon: Rest, monitor for warning signs (nausea, confusion, chest discomfort), contact clinic if symptoms persist.
routine.evening: Light hydration and easily digestible nourishment; confirm access to emergency contacts.
routine.bedtime: Ensure family or care partners are informed of your condition; have emergency numbers ready.

urgent.insight: Acute hyperglycemic or hypoglycemic emergencies require immediate professional evaluation to prevent life-threatening complications such as Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA) or Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State (HHS).

interview.insightPregnantTitle: Pregnancy noted — adjusting what I check
interview.insightPregnantText: Gestational diabetes is screened with stricter thresholds. A couple of pregnancy questions follow, and your labs will be read against pregnancy ranges.
interview.insightT1dText: Weight loss together with intense thirst and frequent urination can point to type 1 diabetes, which can develop quickly. This will be flagged for clinician review.
interview.insightTriadText: Intense thirst, frequent urination and constant hunger together are the classic trio (polydipsia, polyuria, polyphagia) — high blood sugar pulls water out of your body. The next questions help me tell which type fits.
interview.insightT2Text: Symptoms that build up over months usually point to type 2 diabetes, where the body still makes insulin but resists it. Signs like dark skin patches, tingling and slow healing matter most here.
interview.insightChildTitle: In children this pattern is urgent
interview.insightChildText: Sudden thirst and urination in a child — especially with new bed-wetting — is a strong type 1 signal. A finger-prick glucose check today is the fastest way to know.
interview.insightKetosisText: Fruity breath or deep, rapid breathing can mean ketones are building up — a sign of insulin shortage. Combined with feeling unwell, this needs urgent medical attention.
interview.insightDkaText: Vomiting or stomach pain with high blood sugar can signal diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) — a medical emergency. If you feel very unwell right now, seek urgent care first; this assessment can wait.
interview.insightCheckTitle: Sign noted — the assessment keeps going
interview.insightCheckText: Stomach pain, vomiting, fruity breath or deep breathing can have many causes, and one sign on its own is not an emergency. The next questions help me tell whether this fits a pattern that needs urgent care.
interview.insightHypoText: Shakiness, sweating or dizziness can mean low blood sugar. If you have a glucose meter, a reading taken now would be valuable evidence.
interview.childProbeHelper: In children, new bed-wetting with extra thirst or urination is the strongest type 1 signal.
interview.t2ProbeHelper: With a slow build-up, these signs strongly point to the type 2 pattern.
interview.insightShortcutTitle: Skipping the lab questions — here is why
interview.insightShortcutText: With the signs you reported, the next step is the same no matter what a lab would say: get checked by a doctor today. I skipped the lab questions to save you time — finish the rest so your report is complete for the clinician.
interview.allAnsweredText: Review your evidence, then run the assessment.

diagnosisResult.preventionIntro: Healthy lifestyle choices can help prevent type 2 diabetes. If you have prediabetes, lifestyle changes may slow the condition or keep it from becoming diabetes.
diagnosisResult.preventionListIntro: A healthy lifestyle includes the following:
diagnosisResult.preventionEatText: Choose foods lower in fat and calories and higher in fiber. Focus on fruits, vegetables and whole grains.
diagnosisResult.preventionActiveText: Aim for 150 or more minutes a week of moderate to vigorous aerobic activity, such as brisk walking, bicycling, running or swimming.
diagnosisResult.preventionWeightText: If you are overweight, losing some weight and keeping it off may slow prediabetes from becoming type 2 diabetes. If you have prediabetes, losing 7% to 10% of your body weight may lower the risk of diabetes.
diagnosisResult.preventionSitText: Sitting for long periods can raise the risk of type 2 diabetes. Get up every 30 minutes and move around for at least a few minutes.
diagnosisResult.preventionMetformin: People with prediabetes may take metformin (Fortamet, Glumetza, others), a diabetes medicine, to lower the risk of type 2 diabetes. This is most often prescribed for older adults who are obese and who can't lower blood sugar levels with lifestyle changes.
diagnosisResult.preventionGdmIntro: During pregnancy your blood-sugar targets are stricter. Gestational diabetes can usually be managed well — and its risks greatly reduced — with early care.
diagnosisResult.preventionGdmWatchText: Test as your obstetric team advises. The 75g OGTT around weeks 24–28 confirms or rules out gestational diabetes — earlier if you have risk factors.
diagnosisResult.preventionGdmEatText: Smaller, regular meals built on whole grains, vegetables and protein help avoid sugar spikes. Ask for a dietitian referral.
diagnosisResult.preventionGdmActiveText: A short walk after meals lowers glucose spikes. Keep to the activity level your doctor approves for your pregnancy.
diagnosisResult.preventionGdmFollowUpText: Gestational diabetes raises your lifetime type 2 risk. Re-test 4–12 weeks after delivery, then every 1–3 years.
diagnosisResult.preventionGdmNote: Any diabetes treatment during pregnancy needs obstetric supervision — never start or stop medication on your own.
diagnosisResult.preventionDiabetesIntro: Your results meet diabetes-level evidence. These steps protect your eyes, kidneys, nerves and heart — the earlier you start, the better.
diagnosisResult.preventionDiabetesDoctorText: Bring these results with you. Diabetes treatment works best when it starts early — your doctor will set targets and a monitoring plan with you.
diagnosisResult.preventionDiabetesLabsText: If you have not had one yet, a fasting glucose or HbA1c test confirms the result and becomes your baseline for tracking.
diagnosisResult.preventionDiabetesBasicsText: The same lifestyle that prevents diabetes also treats it: healthy food, 150 minutes of activity a week, and a steady weight.
diagnosisResult.preventionDiabetesCheckText: Ask your doctor about eye, kidney, foot and blood-pressure checks — catching problems early prevents lasting damage.
diagnosisResult.preventionDiabetesNote: Urgent warning signs — vomiting, fruity breath, deep rapid breathing, or confusion — need emergency care straight away.
diagnosisResult.preventionRiskIntro: No diabetes yet — but your risk factors make prevention worthwhile. Small, steady changes cut the risk sharply.
diagnosisResult.preventionRiskMoveText: Brisk walking, cycling or swimming — anything that raises your breathing — is the single most effective habit.
diagnosisResult.preventionRiskWeightText: If you are overweight, losing 5–10% of your body weight measurably improves blood sugar and blood pressure.
diagnosisResult.preventionRiskFoodText: Build meals around vegetables, whole grains and lean protein; go easy on sugary drinks and processed snacks.
diagnosisResult.preventionRiskScreenText: With risk factors, screen for diabetes every 1–3 years — sooner if prediabetes is ever found.

plainSummary.title: In short
plainSummary.whatThisIs: This report compares your answers with common patterns of diabetes. It is a screening — not a final diagnosis. A doctor and a simple test can confirm.
plainSummary.matchedMany: Your answers matched {{count}} common sign(s) associated with high blood sugar.
plainSummary.matchedFew: This run included little direct evidence — the result leans on general risk patterns.
plainSummary.couldFitTwo: The signs could fit {{first}} ({{firstPercent}}%) or {{second}} ({{secondPercent}}%) — the first steps are the same either way.
plainSummary.noType: No single diabetes type pattern stood out yet.

excessiveThirst.meaning: Can occur when blood glucose is high — the body pulls water to dilute the sugar.
excessiveThirst.prevention: Drink water regularly and keep blood sugar in the target range; avoid sugary drinks.

frequentUrination.meaning: Often accompanies high blood glucose — the kidneys flush out the extra sugar.
frequentUrination.prevention: Limit caffeine in the evening and keep glucose well controlled to reduce night-time trips.

excessiveHunger.meaning: Can occur when glucose cannot effectively enter cells.
excessiveHunger.prevention: Eat balanced meals with fibre and protein so energy is released slowly.

weightLoss.meaning: The body burns fat and muscle for energy when glucose can't enter cells.
weightLoss.prevention: See a doctor soon — sudden weight loss needs checking; balanced meals help rebuild healthy weight.

fatigue.meaning: Cells don't get enough glucose for energy.
fatigue.prevention: Light regular exercise, good sleep and steady meals help restore energy.

blurredVision.meaning: High glucose draws water into the eye's lens, blurring focus.
blurredVision.prevention: Bring glucose back to target and get an eye exam — vision usually improves as sugar stabilises.

slowHealing.meaning: High glucose slows blood flow and weakens immune repair.
slowHealing.prevention: Clean and protect wounds early and keep glucose in range to speed up healing.

tingling.meaning: High glucose can irritate small nerve fibres over time.
tingling.prevention: Check your feet daily and keep glucose steady to protect the nerves from further damage.

frequentInfections.meaning: High glucose weakens the immune system's defences.
frequentInfections.prevention: Keep glucose in range, keep skin clean and dry, and treat infections early.

acanthosisNigricans.meaning: Dark, velvety skin patches — commonly linked with insulin resistance.
acanthosisNigricans.prevention: Weight loss and exercise often fade these patches — ask a doctor about insulin resistance.

irritability.meaning: Blood sugar swings can affect mood and concentration.
irritability.prevention: Steady meals, sleep and glucose control can lift mood — seek support if it persists.

recurrentInfections.meaning: Glucose in urine feeds bacteria and yeast.
recurrentInfections.prevention: Control sugar levels, stay hydrated, and see a doctor for infections that keep coming back.

bedWetting.meaning: Extra glucose pulls more water — a classic Type 1 sign in children.
bedWetting.prevention: A quick glucose check today can rule out early diabetes — see a doctor promptly.

fruityBreath.meaning: Possible diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) — seek care urgently.
fruityBreath.prevention: This can signal DKA (a dangerous chemical imbalance) — check ketones and seek urgent care.

deepRapidBreathing.meaning: The body tries to release ketone acids — seek care urgently.
deepRapidBreathing.prevention: An emergency sign (possible DKA) — go to emergency care immediately.

nausea.meaning: Can occur when blood glucose or ketones are very high.
nausea.prevention: Sip water slowly and seek care if it persists — nausea with high sugar can be serious.

vomiting.meaning: With very high glucose this can signal DKA — seek care urgently.
vomiting.prevention: Seek medical care quickly — vomiting with high glucose risks dehydration and DKA.

abdominalPain.meaning: With very high glucose this can signal DKA — seek care urgently.
abdominalPain.prevention: Get medical help promptly, especially with vomiting or high sugar — possible DKA.

sweating.meaning: Can be a warning sign of low blood sugar (hypoglycemia).
sweating.prevention: Check blood sugar — sweating can signal a low; keep fast-acting sugar within reach.

shaking.meaning: Common warning sign of low blood sugar (hypoglycemia).
shaking.prevention: Test glucose now — trembling often means low sugar; use the 15/15 rule if below 70 mg/dL.

dizziness.meaning: Can come from low — or very high — blood sugar.
dizziness.prevention: Sit down and check glucose; treat lows quickly and seek help if it is severe.

education.careTitle: Can it be reversed / What to do
education.disclaimer: Educational background only — always follow your healthcare provider's advice.

no_strong_indication.name: Normal Healthy Range
no_strong_indication.tagline: Your biomarkers and symptoms show no significant signs of diabetes.
what: Your blood sugar levels are within normal reference ranges (Fasting glucose < 100 mg/dL, HbA1c < 5.7%).
Your body's cells are properly using insulin to process glucose from food.
No acute or classic diabetic symptoms were reported in this assessment.
Routine preventive screening helps ensure your metabolism stays healthy over time.
causes: Healthy insulin sensitivity: Your cells absorb glucose efficiently from the bloodstream.
Balanced metabolism: Your liver and pancreas are regulating blood sugar smoothly.
Absence of acute genetic, hormonal, or environmental diabetes risk triggers.
symptoms: Normal sustained daily energy levels without unusual fatigue.
Absence of excessive thirst (polydipsia) or frequent urination (polyuria).
Stable body weight and healthy wound healing response.
care: Continue eating balanced, nutrient-rich meals with vegetables, whole grains, and lean proteins.
Maintain at least 150 minutes of moderate physical activity every week.
Schedule regular annual checkups to keep tracking your health numbers.
Re-screen if you ever experience unexplained weight loss or persistent thirst.

prediabetes.name: Prediabetes
prediabetes.tagline: Blood sugar is elevated above normal — but not yet diabetes. This stage is reversible.
what: Blood glucose levels are higher than normal (Fasting 100–125 mg/dL or HbA1c 5.7–6.4%).
It indicates your cells are beginning to resist insulin, causing excess sugar to stay in the blood.
It is an early warning stage: without changes, up to 70% of people with prediabetes develop Type 2 diabetes.
Importantly, prediabetes can often be completely reversed with lifestyle adjustments.
causes: Insulin resistance: Muscle, fat, and liver cells stop responding effectively to insulin, forcing the pancreas to work overtime.
Excess abdominal body weight: Visceral fat around the organs releases inflammatory signals that block insulin action.
Sedentary lifestyle: Inactive muscles consume less glucose and become resistant to insulin.
Genetics and family history: Having a parent or sibling with diabetes increases your biological predisposition.
Diet high in refined carbs and sweetened drinks: Frequent glucose spikes place constant stress on the pancreas.
symptoms: Prediabetes is usually silent — most people feel completely normal for years.
Acanthosis nigricans: Darkened, velvety skin patches on the neck, armpits, or groin.
Mild post-meal sluggishness or afternoon energy crashes.
Slightly increased thirst or urination in some individuals.
care: High reversal potential: Losing just 5–7% of your body weight lowers the risk of developing diabetes by 58%.
Engage in at least 150 minutes of moderate activity weekly (e.g., 30 minutes of brisk walking 5 days a week).
Swap refined sugars, sodas, and white bread for leafy greens, legumes, whole grains, and lean protein.
Re-check laboratory glucose biomarkers every 6 to 12 months with your doctor.

type2.name: Type 2 Diabetes
type2.tagline: The most common form of diabetes — cells resist insulin, causing persistent high blood sugar.
what: Cells do not respond normally to insulin (insulin resistance), and the pancreas cannot produce enough to overcome it.
Diagnostic criteria: Fasting glucose ≥ 126 mg/dL or HbA1c ≥ 6.5% on multiple tests.
Over time, untreated high blood glucose can damage blood vessels, nerves, eyes, heart, and kidneys.
Effective medical management, medications, and lifestyle changes can control it and prevent complications.
causes: Progressive insulin resistance coupled with gradual decline in pancreatic beta-cell insulin secretion.
Excess body weight and high visceral fat percentage.
Strong genetic predisposition and family medical history.
Chronic inflammation, poor sleep, long-term stress, and age over 35–45.
symptoms: Frequent urination, particularly waking up multiple times during the night (polyuria).
Persistent, unquenchable thirst (polydipsia) and constant dry mouth.
Persistent fatigue, sluggishness, and blurred vision.
Slow-healing cuts, tingling or numbness in feet or fingers.
care: Consult your physician promptly for personalized medical management and medication (e.g. Metformin).
Adopt structured medical nutrition therapy focusing on low glycemic index foods.
Monitor blood glucose levels as recommended by your healthcare provider.
Undergo annual clinical screenings for retinal eye health, kidney function, and foot nerve circulation.

type1.name: Type 1 Diabetes
type1.tagline: An autoimmune condition where the body's immune system stops insulin production.
what: An autoimmune disorder where the immune system mistakenly attacks the insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas.
Without insulin, glucose cannot enter cells for energy and accumulates to dangerous levels in the blood.
It often starts in children, teens, or young adults — but can appear at any age.
It is not caused by diet, sugar intake, or lifestyle, and cannot be prevented.
causes: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells by self-reactive T-cells.
Genetic susceptibility combined with environmental triggers (such as viral infections).
It is not caused by lifestyle, diet, or lack of exercise.
symptoms: Rapid onset of severe thirst, extreme hunger, and frequent urination.
Sudden unexplained weight loss despite eating normally or more.
Extreme exhaustion, weakness, and blurry vision.
Emergency signs (DKA): Fruity breath, nausea, vomiting, rapid deep breathing, abdominal pain — seek emergency care immediately.
care: Daily insulin therapy for life via multiple daily injections or continuous insulin pump.
Frequent blood glucose monitoring (fingersticks or continuous glucose monitor / CGM).
Carbohydrate counting to match insulin doses with meals.
Regular follow-ups with an endocrinologist.

gestational.name: Gestational Diabetes
gestational.tagline: Elevated blood sugar that first develops during pregnancy.
what: Hormones produced by the placenta interfere with insulin, leading to insulin resistance during pregnancy.
Typically diagnosed through oral glucose tolerance testing (OGTT) around the 24th to 28th week of pregnancy.
Usually resolves after giving birth, but increases future risk for Type 2 diabetes.
Proper management protects both the mother's health and baby's safe development.
causes: Placental hormones (such as human placental lactogen) naturally increasing insulin resistance.
Inability of the maternal pancreas to produce 2–3 times more insulin to meet pregnancy demands.
Risk increases with maternal age over 25, pre-pregnancy BMI ≥ 25, PCOS, or family diabetes history.
symptoms: Most expectant mothers feel zero symptoms — which is why routine prenatal screening is standard.
Mild fatigue, unusual thirst, or slightly increased urination beyond typical pregnancy changes.
care: Follow a balanced prenatal meal plan guided by a clinical dietitian.
Engage in doctor-approved gentle activity such as walking or prenatal swimming.
Monitor blood sugar daily before and after meals.
Insulin or safe oral medications if diet and exercise do not keep glucose within targets.

general.name: Diabetes Spectrum
general.tagline: Understanding blood sugar regulation and metabolic health.
what: Insulin is a hormone made by the pancreas that allows glucose to enter your cells for energy.
When insulin is absent or ineffective, glucose remains trapped in the blood, leading to high blood sugar.
Chronic hyperglycemia can affect blood vessels, circulation, heart, and vital organs over time.
Early identification and proactive care significantly improve long-term outcomes.
causes: Varies by condition: Autoimmune (Type 1), metabolic & lifestyle (Type 2/Prediabetes), or hormonal (Gestational).
Complex interaction of genetics, physical activity, nutrition, and body composition.
symptoms: Increased thirst, frequent urination, fatigue, and blurred vision.
Tingling in extremities or slow-healing cuts.
care: Laboratory diagnostic testing: Fasting plasma glucose, HbA1c, or OGTT.
Adopting nutrient-dense eating patterns and consistent weekly movement.
Partnering with a licensed healthcare provider for tailored medical guidance.

familyHistory.meaning: A parent or sibling with diabetes raises your lifetime risk — screening should start earlier and repeat regularly.

obesity.meaning: Excess body fat — especially around the waist — makes the body resistant to insulin, the top driver of type 2 diabetes.

overweight.meaning: A BMI of 25–30 already raises type 2 risk; a modest 5–10% weight loss brings it down sharply.

hypertension.meaning: High blood pressure often travels with high sugar and doubles the risk to the heart and kidneys.

sedentaryLifestyle.meaning: Sitting most of the day weakens glucose control — 150 minutes of movement a week cuts risk by about a third.

gestationalHistory.meaning: Diabetes during pregnancy means a high chance of type 2 later in life — test every 1–3 years.

smoking.meaning: Smoking worsens insulin resistance and damages blood vessels — quitting is the single best step.

highCholesterol.meaning: High cholesterol together with high sugar speeds up artery damage — diet, movement and medication help.

pcosHistory.meaning: PCOS is strongly linked to insulin resistance — women with PCOS need regular glucose checks.

ethnicityHighRisk.meaning: Some ethnic groups (South Asian, Southeast Asian and others) face higher risk at lower weights — screen earlier.
